summary: Moonsill helps lunar mission planners compare landing sites and touchdown times near the Moon’s south pole. It combines JPL Horizons ephemerides with NASA LOLA elevation data to estimate when the Sun and Earth are visible above the local terrain. Users set operational requirements, test a range of touchdown delays, and see which requirement fails first. The app explains the result with timelines and terrain cross-sections and compares changes to the landing date, site, or requirements. In our reference case, the original plan met all requirements but tolerated only 117.5 hours of delay out of the requested 168. An independent calculation showed that terrain resolution could change the verdict for one alternative, so Moonsill reports that uncertainty alongside the recommendation.
details:
Moonsill is an interactive planning tool for comparing candidate landing sites and touchdown times at the lunar south pole. Users choose a location and time, define the sunlight and Earth visibility needed for their first surface operations, and test how delays affect those requirements.

The app uses topocentric Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons and computes the local horizon from NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA elevation data, accounting for lunar curvature. It displays visibility windows, flags uncertainty where terrain coverage or resolution limits the analysis, and shows the terrain responsible for a selected event. Users can compare a later touchdown, another candidate site, or a change to a requirement that they explicitly allow. They can also share a scenario or export its inputs and results as JSON.

Our reference mission needed 72 hours of continuous sunlight from touchdown, at least one 24-hour Earth visibility window, and no Earth visibility gap longer than 120 hours during the first 14 days. The nominal plan passed, but delaying touchdown by five days caused the Earth gap requirement to fail. Moonsill identifies the limiting event and shows how a different site or time changes the result.

We cross-checked the reference case using Skyfield and NAIF SPICE, a separate terrain calculation, and one-minute delay sampling. For one same-site alternative, the recommended time passed with 80 m terrain and failed with 20 m terrain near the landing point because sunrise occurred later. A later candidate passed on both tested terrain grids at every sampled delay from 0 to 168 hours. The app surfaces the measured discrepancy so users can judge the recommendation in context.

We built the backend in Python with FastAPI and the interface in React and TypeScript. The project is deployed on Render using Docker. Its intended use is preliminary planning for surface operations. Earth visibility represents geometric line of sight. Verifying an actual radio link requires ground-station, antenna, and link-budget data.
dataRefs: JPL Horizons System — Sun and Earth ephemerides
NASA LRO LOLA — Lunar South Pole DEMs, 80 m and 20 m (PGDA Product 90)
NASA Lunar Polar Illumination — Long-term Sun and Earth visibility maps (PGDA Product 69)
NASA JPL NAIF SPICE — Kernels for independent verification
NASA LOLA — High-Resolution Topography for Lunar South Pole Sites (PGDA Product 78)
